title: My Years with General Motors
author: Alfred P. Sloan Jr.
theme: A large company works best when operations are decentralised to responsible divisions while policy and financial control are coordinated from the centre.
summary: Alfred Sloan led General Motors for more than three decades, first as president and then as chairman. This book is his account of how he turned a loose collection of car and parts companies into the largest industrial enterprise of its time. It reads less like a memoir than a case study in building management structures.

When Sloan rose to the top in the early 1920s, the company had grown quickly through acquisitions but lacked any real system. Divisions bought and spent as they pleased, nobody had an accurate picture of inventories or cash, and a sharp business slump nearly broke the firm. Sloan's response was a principle he called decentralised operations with coordinated control.

Each division ran its own business and was judged on its results, but the central office set policy, allocated capital and watched performance. Uniform accounting, return on investment, sales forecasts and regular reports from dealers gave top management facts instead of guesses. Committees brought division heads and staff experts together to agree policy, while day-to-day execution stayed in the divisions.

Sloan also rethought the product line. Rather than offering one standard car, General Motors arranged its brands in a ladder of price ranges, from Chevrolet at the bottom to Cadillac at the top, so that buyers could move up as their incomes grew. Combined with yearly model changes, attention to styling, consumer credit and trade-ins, this strategy overtook Ford's single, unchanging Model T.
The book is candid about mistakes. A heavily promoted air-cooled engine project failed, and Sloan used it to show the danger of forcing an idea on divisions without evidence.
His core message is that good management relies on objective facts, clear responsibility and a balance between freedom for the parts and discipline from the whole.
takeaway: Give units real autonomy, but bind them together with common policy, shared financial measures and decisions based on facts.

questions.q: What organising principle did Sloan apply to General Motors?
options: Full centralisation of every decision at headquarters
Decentralised operations with coordinated control
Complete independence for each division with no central oversight
Management by a single founder-owner
questions.why: Sloan let divisions run their own operations while the centre coordinated policy, capital and performance measurement.

questions.q: What problem did General Motors face when Sloan began reorganising it in the early 1920s?
options: It had too few products to sell
It was a small family firm with no capital
It had grown through acquisitions without adequate controls over spending and inventory
It was barred from selling cars outside the United States
questions.why: Rapid, loosely managed expansion left the company without reliable information, and a slump exposed the weakness.

questions.q: How did Sloan's product strategy differ from Ford's approach with the Model T?
options: GM offered a range of cars at different price levels for different buyers
GM concentrated on a single low-cost model
GM sold only luxury cars
GM stopped changing its models
questions.why: Sloan built a ladder of brands spanning price ranges, whereas Ford relied on one standard car.

questions.q: Which brand sat at the bottom of GM's price ladder in Sloan's strategy?
options: Cadillac
Buick
Oldsmobile
Chevrolet
questions.why: Chevrolet was the entry-level brand, with Cadillac at the top of the range.

questions.q: Which financial measure did Sloan rely on to judge the performance of divisions?
options: Number of employees
Return on investment
Total floor space of factories
Advertising spend
questions.why: Return on investment let the centre compare divisions on a common basis and allocate capital accordingly.

questions.q: What lesson did Sloan draw from the failed air-cooled engine project?
options: Engineering research should be abandoned
Divisions should never cooperate with the central research staff
Ideas should not be forced on operating divisions without solid evidence
Only the chairman should make engineering decisions
questions.why: The episode showed the cost of pushing an unproven idea on divisions instead of deciding on facts.

questions.q: What role did committees play in Sloan's management system?
options: They brought division leaders and staff experts together to agree on policy
They handled all daily production decisions
They replaced the need for any chief executive
They existed only for social purposes
questions.why: Committees formed policy jointly, while execution remained with the divisions.

questions.q: Which practice helped GM attract buyers in a market that was becoming saturated?
options: Refusing trade-ins
Keeping one design unchanged for many years
Selling only for cash
Annual model changes and attention to styling
questions.why: Regular model updates and styling gave customers reasons to upgrade once most buyers already owned a car.

questions.q: Why did Sloan want uniform accounting and regular forecasts across divisions?
options: To reduce the number of dealers
So top management could base decisions on objective facts
To avoid paying taxes
To let each division hide its results
questions.why: Consistent data allowed the central office to compare, control and plan without relying on guesswork.

questions.q: What balance does the book present as the core of good management in a large firm?
options: Speed over accuracy
Marketing over engineering
Freedom for operating units combined with discipline from the centre
Seniority over performance
questions.why: Sloan's system rests on combining divisional autonomy with coordinated policy and financial control.
